title: Making electric cars exciting, and then affordable
problem: Before Tesla, electric cars were seen as slow, short-range and boring. Big car makers were not betting on them.
innovation: Start with an expensive, exciting sports car. Use the money and learning to build cheaper cars, step by step.
overview: Tesla builds electric cars, batteries and solar and energy-storage products. It started in 2003 and is now one of the best-known car makers in the world.
model: Sells cars directly to customers (not through dealers), plus energy storage and solar products. Cars get new features through software updates over the internet.
technology: Battery packs, electric motors, car software, and its own fast-charging network.
milestones: Roadster production begins; new CEO as funds run low
Patents opened for others to use
Model 3 unveiled; battery Gigafactory starts producing
advantages: Early focus on batteries and software
challenges: Building cars at scale is hard and capital-intensive
lesson: Start with a small premium market, learn, then expand to a larger one.
lessons: Be ready to survive the hard years
future: Cheaper batteries could affect transport and energy storage. This is an open question, not a prediction.

references.title: Tesla Annual Report to Shareholders, FY2023 (SEC)

points: Tesla was founded in 2003 by Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning. Elon Musk joined in 2004 as chairman and early investor.
The first car, the Roadster, was unveiled in 2006 and went into production in 2008.
Musk became CEO in 2008, when the company was close to running out of money.
Over the next years Tesla added the Model S (2012) and the Model 3 (2017), aimed at more people.
In 2006 Tesla published a plan: build a low-volume sports car, use that money for a medium-priced car, then an even cheaper one.
It also planned to offer zero-emission electric power products.
This step-by-step plan is a key reason people study Tesla: start small, learn, grow.

story.h: How it made money and grew
points: Sells cars directly online and in its own stores, so it controls price and the buying experience.
Sells batteries for homes and power companies, and solar products.
Builds its own fast-charging stations, so owners can travel far. By 2014 it already ran about 97 stations across the US, according to one report.
Opened its patents for others to use in 2014, to help the whole electric car market grow.
2008: the company was close to collapse before new funding arrived.
Scaling the Model 3 in 2017 was very hard; the CEO himself called it 'production hell'.
Regulators have investigated safety claims about its driver-assist features.
Many big car makers now sell electric cars.
In 2016 it started producing batteries at its Gigafactory near Reno, Nevada, to cut battery costs.
A factory in Shanghai began operating around 2019, to serve more markets.
It joined the S&P 500 stock index in December 2020.
Start with a small market that will pay more, then go bigger.
Own the parts that matter most (batteries, software).
Say your plan publicly and keep to it, but be ready to fix problems fast.
Cheaper batteries could make electric cars normal in more countries.
Self-driving is promised but not solved. Treat timelines with care.
More rivals mean prices and profits may be squeezed.

think: Why did Tesla begin with an expensive car and not a cheap one?
What parts of your own plan should you control yourself?

title: From graphics chips to AI computing
problem: Graphics chips were used mainly for games.
innovation: Make GPUs programmable for general computing with CUDA.
overview: NVIDIA designs chips and software. It was founded in 1993.
model: Designs chips and sells chips, systems and software.
technology: GPUs and the CUDA programming platform.
milestones: GeForce 256 marketed as the first GPU
challenges: Depends on outside manufacturers; competition and export rules
lesson: Software tools can make hardware much more valuable.
future: Demand for AI computing may shape chip design. This is uncertain.

title: Making rockets reusable and space cheaper
problem: Rockets were thrown away after one flight, like throwing away a jet after one trip. That made space very costly.
innovation: Build rockets whose first stage can land and fly again, and build most parts in-house.
overview: SpaceX designs, builds and launches rockets and spacecraft, and runs the Starlink satellite internet service. It was founded in 2002.
model: Sells launch services to NASA, governments and companies. Also sells satellite internet subscriptions (Starlink).
technology: Reusable Falcon 9 boosters, Dragon spacecraft, Starlink satellites and the Starship rocket under test.
milestones: Falcon 1 reaches orbit on its fourth try
Dragon docks with the space station
First reflight of an orbital-class booster
Crew Dragon carries astronauts to the station
Starship test flights continue, with mixed results
advantages: Reuse can lower the cost of launches
lesson: Repeated testing and learning from failures can solve hard problems.
future: Cheaper launch could make more space projects practical. This is uncertain.

points: SpaceX was founded in 2002 by Elon Musk.
Its first three Falcon 1 launches failed. The fourth, in September 2008, reached orbit. It was the first privately built liquid-fuel rocket to do so.
Later rockets, Falcon 9 (first launch in 2010) and Dragon, became NASA's partners for flights to the space station.

story.h: The big idea: land the rocket
points: In December 2015 a Falcon 9 first stage landed upright after reaching orbit.
In April 2016 a booster landed on a ship at sea.
On 30 March 2017 SpaceX flew an orbital-class booster for the second time.

story.h: How it made money and grew
points: NASA contracts for cargo and astronaut flights gave steady income.
In May 2012 Dragon became the first commercial spacecraft to deliver cargo to the space station and return.
In 2020 Crew Dragon carried NASA astronauts to the station.
Starlink began launching in large batches (60 satellites at once) in May 2019 to sell internet from space.
Three early launch failures nearly ended the company.
A Falcon 9 exploded during a 2015 cargo mission, and another rocket was destroyed in a test on the pad in 2016.
Starship test flights have had explosions and lost spacecraft, for example in March 2025.
Reusing rockets became a goal for other launch companies too.
Falcon Heavy's first flight in February 2018 landed two of three boosters.
More satellites are launched each year, which also raises worries about crowded orbits.
Test, fail, learn and fix, then test again.
Attack the biggest cost, not the small ones.
Build key parts yourself if buying them blocks your speed.
Starship is designed to carry much more and to be fully reusable. It is still in testing.
If launch becomes cheaper, more science and internet projects become possible.
Rules for space traffic and space junk are still developing.

think: Why did SpaceX focus on landing the first stage?
How is learning from failure different from hiding failure?

title: From DVDs by mail to streaming
problem: Renting movies meant going to a store and paying late fees.
innovation: Rent DVDs by mail with no late fees, then move to streaming over the internet.
overview: Netflix is an entertainment company founded in 1997.
model: Customers pay a regular subscription to watch content.
technology: Internet video streaming and recommendation software.
challenges: Competition from many other streaming services
Content is costly to produce or license
lesson: Be ready to change your own business when technology changes.
future: Internet speed and devices keep changing how people watch. How it will end up is uncertain.

title: Selling computing power as a service
problem: Starting a website or app meant buying and running your own servers.
innovation: Rent computing and storage over the internet and pay only for what you use.
overview: Amazon Web Services (AWS) is the cloud computing business of Amazon.
model: Customers pay for usage of computing, storage and other services.
technology: Large data centres and software that shares them among many customers.
challenges: Strong competition from other cloud providers
Customers worry about outages and costs
lesson: A tool built for your own needs can become a product for others.
lessons: Lower the cost of starting for others
future: More software may run in the cloud. The exact path is uncertain.

title: From a college website to a family of apps
problem: People wanted an easy, always-on way to stay in touch with friends, family and communities.
innovation: A social network that spread from one campus to the world, then added photos, messaging and VR through its own products and acquisitions.
overview: Meta Platforms owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Threads and virtual-reality products. It began in 2004 as a college website and was renamed Meta in 2021.
model: Free apps for users. The company earns almost all its money by showing ads (about 98% of revenue in 2023, according to public data).
technology: Large-scale software systems, AI that recommends content and ads, and virtual and augmented reality hardware.
advantages: Very large user base across several apps
challenges: Concerns about privacy and harmful content
Regulators in many countries are watching it closely
Its VR and metaverse bets are long-term and uncertain
lesson: Buying or building products that people use daily can make a company strong, but trust and privacy must be earned.
lessons: Network effects: more users make an app more useful
Ads can fund free products, but people care about data
Do not depend on one product
future: VR, AR and AI may change how people connect. Whether people will adopt them widely is uncertain.

points: Mark Zuckerberg started the site in 2004 from a Harvard dorm. It was first called TheFacebook.
It was renamed Facebook in 2005 and grew far beyond the campus.
In 2012 it bought Instagram. In 2014 it bought WhatsApp and Oculus (VR).
In October 2021 the parent company was renamed Meta Platforms to focus on the 'metaverse'.

story.h: The big idea: the network effect
points: The more of your friends use an app, the more useful it is for you.
Meta kept buying or building apps people use every day.
Free apps bring huge numbers of users, and ads pay for it.

story.h: How it made money and grew
points: Ads are matched to people's interests using data and AI.
Advertising was about 97.8% of revenue in 2023 and is around 98 to 99% in the Family of Apps segment in 2025, according to public summaries.
Reality Labs (VR and AR) has a small revenue (about $2.2 billion in 2025 per one summary) and has run at a loss.
Privacy: in 2016 the company had to pause data sharing between Facebook and WhatsApp in the European Union.
Regulators in many countries have questioned how it handles data and harmful content.
Spending on the metaverse has been very high, and the payoff is uncertain.
Social networks changed how people share news, photos and opinions.
Small businesses can reach customers cheaply with ads on its apps.
Ideas of online privacy and responsibility are now part of the public debate.
Products that connect people can grow very fast.
Free for users can still be a strong business if someone else (advertisers) pays.
Trust is hard to win back once it is lost.
AI assistants inside messaging apps.
Smart glasses and VR may become everyday devices, but it is not guaranteed.
Stricter rules on data and teen safety are likely in many countries.

think: Who is the customer: the user, or the advertiser?
What would you do to earn trust if you ran a social app?

title: Organising the world's information
problem: In the 1990s the web was growing fast but finding good pages was slow and the results were often poor.
innovation: A search method called PageRank that ranked a page higher when many other trusted pages linked to it.
overview: Google runs the world's most used search engine and products like Gmail, YouTube, Android and Chrome. It was founded in 1998 and is part of the company Alphabet.
model: Most income comes from ads shown with search results and on partner sites. It also sells cloud services and subscriptions.
technology: Search ranking, huge data centres, Android, machine learning and cloud computing.
milestones: Transformer paper published by Google researchers
US court rules Google illegally holds a search monopoly
Court orders data sharing; no forced sale of Chrome
advantages: Huge amounts of data and computing power
Products used by billions of people
challenges: Antitrust and regulatory cases in several countries
New AI products compete with search
lesson: Solve one clear problem very well, then use that trust to build many products.
lessons: Free tools can build large audiences
future: AI may change how people search and find answers. How this will play out is uncertain.

references.title: NPR/WAMC: Judge lets Google keep Chrome (Sept 2025)

points: Larry Page and Sergey Brin, students at Stanford, founded Google in 1998.
Their ranking idea gave clearly better results than other search sites.
The company added Gmail (2004), bought YouTube (2006), and released Chrome and Android (2008).
In 2015 Alphabet was created as a parent company for Google and other bets.

story.h: The big idea: useful and simple
points: A very plain search page that loaded fast.
Ads were relevant to what you searched. AdWords launched in 2000.
More users made the ad business stronger.

story.h: How it made money and grew
points: Ads on search and other products are the main income.
Android spread Google services to billions of phones.
Cloud and YouTube subscriptions add other income.
In August 2024 a US judge ruled that Google illegally keeps a monopoly in search.
On 2 September 2025 the judge did not order a sale of Chrome or Android, but ordered Google to share some search data with rivals and to stop exclusive default deals.
Google said it would appeal, so the story is not over.
People expect any answer in seconds.
Research from Google, such as the 2017 Transformer paper, helped start today's AI language models.
Online advertising became a large business.
Do one thing exceptionally well first.
Better quality can beat bigger budgets.
Success also attracts rules and scrutiny.
AI answers may change how people search.
Rules about default settings and data sharing may reshape competition.
Both are still developing.

think: Why did a simple search page beat busier rivals?
How could AI change the way ads work?

title: Bringing AI chat to everyone
problem: Strong AI research stayed mostly with experts. Ordinary people had no easy way to try it.
innovation: A simple chat window (ChatGPT) that lets anyone talk to a large language model in plain language.
overview: OpenAI is an AI research and product company, best known for ChatGPT. It was founded in December 2015.
model: Free and paid plans for users, plus paid access for developers and companies.
technology: Large language models trained on very large amounts of text, and very large computing power.
milestones: GPT-4 released; CEO briefly removed and returned
Restructured into OpenAI Group PBC under the OpenAI Foundation
advantages: Early lead in popular AI chat products
Close ties to large computing partners
challenges: Training and running AI costs a lot
Debates over safety, copyright and how the company is governed
lesson: A simple interface can bring a hard technology to millions of people.
lessons: Make the product easy to try
Research and product need each other
New technology brings new rules and debates
future: AI assistants may become part of many jobs and tools. Their limits and rules are still being worked out.

references.title: AP via Washington Times: OpenAI new structure

points: OpenAI began in 2015 as a non-profit research lab.
In 2019 it added a 'capped-profit' company to raise money for expensive computing, and Microsoft invested.
GPT-3 (June 2020) showed what big language models could do.
ChatGPT, released in late 2022, reached over a million sign-ups within five days, according to OpenAI.

story.h: The big idea: make it easy to try
points: The technology already existed. The chat interface made it usable for everyone.
People used it to write, learn, code and brainstorm.
This brought AI into daily conversation worldwide.

story.h: How it made money and grew
points: Subscriptions for individuals and teams.
Selling access to its models for developers and companies.
Microsoft became a large partner and investor (reported $10 billion in 2023) and put OpenAI-based tools into its products.
November 2023: the board briefly removed CEO Sam Altman, then he returned within days.
Running AI costs a lot of computing money.
Writers and publishers have sued over how AI is trained, and safety debates continue.
Many companies launched their own AI assistants.
Schools and workplaces are still deciding how to use AI.
On 28 October 2025 it completed a restructuring: the for-profit became OpenAI Group PBC, controlled by the non-profit OpenAI Foundation. Microsoft holds about 27%, according to reports.
A simple product can unlock a hard technology.
Big technology needs big money, and that shapes how a company is organised.
Early users teach you what the product is really for.
AI assistants might handle more tasks for people.
Questions about copyright, jobs, safety and rules are still open.
No one can say for sure how far the technology will go.

think: Why did a chat window matter more than a better model?
What would you never want an AI to do for you?

title: Making mobile internet cheap in India
problem: Mobile data in India was costly and slow. Many people could not afford to use the internet much.
innovation: A new network built for 4G data from day one, with free voice calls and very low data prices.
overview: Reliance Jio is an Indian telecom company, part of Reliance Industries. It launched commercially on 5 September 2016.
model: Sells data and phone plans, and builds digital services (apps, devices, fibre) on top of its network.
technology: A 4G network using voice over LTE, towers and fibre across the country.
milestones: JioPhone announced; free offer ends in March
Facebook and Google invest in Jio Platforms
advantages: Built on new technology from day one
Low prices attracted many first-time internet users
challenges: Building a network needs very large investment
Price competition with other telecom firms
lesson: A big drop in price can unlock a whole new group of users.
lessons: Build for the market's biggest gap
Use the network to launch other services
future: Cheap data helped digital payments, video and apps grow in India. What comes next with 5G is uncertain.

references.title: TechRadar: Google to invest in Jio Platforms
Scroll.in: Jio's cheap data and its cost

points: Jio launched on 5 September 2016 with free services at first, later extended to March 2017.
It reached 100 million customers in about six months, according to reports.
In 2017 it announced the JioPhone for people moving up from basic phones.

story.h: The big idea: price as innovation
points: Data was the main product, not voice.
In 2015 one GB cost about 225 rupees. By March 2017 one analysis put the average price across operators at about $0.33 per GB.
Rivals Airtel, Vodafone and Idea had to cut data prices.

story.h: How it made money and grew
points: Free offers brought millions of first-time users.
Monthly data use in India rose from about 200 million GB (June 2016) to 1.3 billion GB (March 2017), according to TeleGeography.
In 2020 Jio Platforms raised money from big investors: Facebook took about 9.99% and Google agreed to invest Rs 33,737 crore for 7.7%.
Building a country-wide network takes very large investment.
Industry income per user fell by about one third (from about Rs 120 to Rs 82.7 a month by March 2017), and weaker rivals struggled or merged.
Critics asked whether very low prices hurt competition in the long run.
Many more people in India use the internet on phones.
Video, payments and apps grew on top of cheaper data.
Operators had to rethink their prices and networks.
Lower the price enough and a whole new group of customers appears.
Build on the newest technology instead of patching the old one.
A big move needs deep pockets and patience.
5G and home broadband may bring faster services.
How profits and competition develop in telecom is still open.
Affordable data is useful only if people also have affordable devices and skills.

think: Who gained and who lost when data prices fell?
Is a free offer a gift or a strategy?

title: Simple messaging for everyone
problem: Texting by SMS cost money and worked differently across countries.
innovation: A simple app that sends messages over the internet on almost any phone, without ads.
overview: WhatsApp is a messaging app used by more than 2 billion people, according to Meta. It was founded in 2009 and is owned by Meta.
model: Early on, a small yearly fee in some countries. Today the app is free and the company grows business tools such as the WhatsApp Business app.
technology: Internet messaging and end-to-end encryption (messages are readable only by sender and receiver).
milestones: Forward limits in India; WhatsApp Business app launched
advantages: Works on many phones and in low-bandwidth places
challenges: Fake news and misinformation can spread fast
lesson: Doing one simple job very well can win billions of users.
future: Messaging apps may become places for shopping, payments and customer service. This is still developing.

references.title: Al Jazeera: WhatsApp limits forwarding in India (2018)

points: Two former Yahoo engineers, Jan Koum and Brian Acton, built WhatsApp in 2009.
Facebook announced it was buying WhatsApp in early 2014 for about $19 billion, according to reports.
Koum left in 2018 and Acton in 2017, reportedly over differences with Facebook.

story.h: The big idea: do one thing well
points: Fast, simple messaging that worked on many phones, even with slow internet.
No games and no ads in the early years.
The focus on simplicity helped it spread by word of mouth.

story.h: How it made money and grew
points: A small fee in some countries in the early years.
After the sale, Meta focused on business messaging: the WhatsApp Business app launched in 2018.
Businesses use it to talk to customers.
In 2016 the company introduced end-to-end encryption for all chats.
In July 2018, after mob killings in India linked to rumours spread on the app, WhatsApp limited forwarding to five chats at a time in India.
Privacy-policy changes have caused debates.
Groups of family, friends and neighbours stay in touch free across the world.
Small shops use it to take orders.
It also shows how fast false news can spread.
A simple tool that solves one daily problem can reach billions.
Privacy can be a feature, not just a rule.
Big reach brings responsibility.
Messaging apps could become places for shopping, payments and support.
How to limit false news without breaking privacy is still debated.
Rules on data and encryption may change.

think: How can an app slow false news and keep chats private?
What small service in your area could use WhatsApp?
